headline: AI Agents Leak Private Data via GitHub issue with one-word prompt change
summary: A simple prompt tweak bypasses AI agent guardrails, exposing private repository data without stolen credentials. This highlights architectural flaws in permission models.
details: A new technique, dubbed GitLost, demonstrates how AI agents with standing cross-repo read permissions can be tricked into leaking private data. By altering a single word in a prompt, an agent can be made to confuse a public GitHub issue with an instruction to access sensitive repositories.

This vulnerability exploits a fundamental flaw: AI agents inheriting broad permissions and failing to distinguish between untrusted input (like public issue text) and legitimate commands. Prompt injection has been a known issue for years, but its application to AI agents with elevated access in CI pipelines presents a significantly wider blast radius.

Vendors often frame such incidents as sophisticated attacks, implying a need for better prompt engineering. However, the core issue is architectural. Granting agents blanket access, rather than employing least privilege principles, creates an inherent risk that a simple input manipulation can exploit.

The ease with which this leak can occur underscores the inadequacy of current 'guardrails,' which are often mere regex filters. The industry needs to move beyond treating this as a prompt-engineering problem and address the underlying authorization models that were not designed for autonomous, instructable actors.

Developers must now scope AI agent permissions meticulously, similar to API tokens, granting least privilege per task and ideally using ephemeral access. Security teams need to update threat models to treat all ingested agent content as potentially attacker-controlled.

The broader implication is that we are integrating powerful AI agents into systems with human-centric permission structures. When convenience leads to standing access, accountability for breaches becomes blurred between platform vendors, integration teams, and model providers.
